title: Joe Robichaux, the Gypsy Tearoom and the Sweethearts of Rhythm
summary: He compares Robichaux's band to Celestin's ballroom style and names visiting territory bands including the Sweethearts of Rhythm, whom he praises.

bands.name: Ina Ray Hutton and Her Orchestra

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: You also played with Joe Robichaux.
He was one of a famous Robichaux family right there in New Orleans. Was his type of music any different from A. J. Piron's or was it sort of a -- I guess what they call it --
He was somewhat like Celestin's band, the ballroom band.
Didn't they call that sweet music sometimes?

Yeah, yeah, right. There used to be a place called -- a tearoom, gypsy tearoom, Little Old Gypsy Tearoom where all the bands played and the visiting bands that would come through like the Carolina Cotton Pickers and Hartley Toots from Miami and Ernie Fields would come in there, too. It was only a few years later that I joined Ernie in New York. And territory bands that'd come through, all girl bands, the bands from Mississippi, from Piney Woods, Sweethearts of Rhythm, that's the name of the band.
Sweethearts of Rhythm -- all girls, yeah.

What was your impression of them, and what was the general impression of the Sweethearts of Rhythm at that time? Did people look at them as a novelty orchestra? You know, what are these gals up here trying to prove or were they taken seriously as musicians because they were accomplished musicians?

Oh, yes, those girls could really wail, the could wail just like the male band. They had a great band with rhythm. In later years, you've heard of the other girl bands, Ina Rae Hutton -- various -- female musicians make a great, great group.
